circumlocution

/sur-kum-loh-KYOO-shun/ - the stress falls on KYOO · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Circumlocution means indirect and wordy language that avoids the point.

Ask Grandpa to borrow the truck and the circumlocution begins: twenty minutes on weather, tires, and responsibility, with never a yes or a no in it.

Example

Dario called the warranty line with one question: covered, or not. Forty minutes of circumlocution later, he had heard about policy tiers, seasonal claim volumes, and the company's founding promise of care — and still could not have said, under oath, whether the repair was covered. He hung up, dialed again, and asked for someone allowed to use short sentences.

Circumlocution is the exact word for what he sat through, because circumlocution means indirect and wordy language that avoids the point — the words circle the answer the way a moth circles a porch light, never landing. A digression wanders off the subject and comes back; circumlocution never leaves the subject and never arrives either.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

wordiness: Wordiness is simply too many words, anywhere, for any reason — a writer who cannot cut, a speaker in love with his own voice. Circumlocution is wordiness with a motive: the extra words exist to keep circling a point the speaker is dodging on purpose.

evasion: Evasion is the dodge itself, managed by any means at all — changing the subject, going silent, leaving the room. Circumlocution is one particular method of evasion: dodging with language, keeping the words flowing around the question so the answer never has to arrive.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

directness: saying the thing straight

bluntness: directness with the cushions removed

Where it sits · how fully the answer is dodged

hedging → circumlocution → stonewalling

hedging vs. circumlocution: Hedging is far milder than circumlocution — a few maybes and mostlys around an answer that does, eventually, arrive; circumlocution keeps talking and never lets the answer arrive at all.

stonewalling vs. circumlocution: Stonewalling goes further than circumlocution — circumlocution at least keeps talking around the point; stonewalling refuses to discuss it at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — circum-: around

Root — locut: spoken (Latin loqui)

Suffix — -ion: the act of

Put it together: Circum- (around) + locut- (spoken) + -ion (the act of) = the act of speaking around. Latin built the word exactly the way the habit works: the talk orbits the point without ever setting down on it.

Use the root in a new word: ventriloquist: Tickets for the ventriloquist's Saturday matinee sold out within the hour.

Circumlocution judges: it says the speaker is dodging on purpose. Plain wordiness is only excess, and hedging is only caution. Keep it apart from this unit's digression — a digression leaves the subject and comes back; circumlocution never leaves the point, and never lands on it either.
